summary: In this episode, the hosts discuss the concept of apocalypse as a biblical genre of revelation, not merely the end of the world. They explore the idea of pre-reflective consciousness (the nous) as a sensory organ for spiritual reality, and how modernity has separated the material and spiritual realms, leading to a reduction of knowledge to language. They argue for a reintegration of the seen and unseen through ritual, worship, and love of neighbor, emphasizing that every action has spiritual significance. The episode includes listener calls on topics such as worship outside the Church, the nature of the nous, and the symbolism of the dove.

concepts.title: Pre-reflective Consciousness
concepts.summary: The level of consciousness before thoughts, which allows one to observe one's own thoughts and self, forming the basis for free will and spiritual growth.

concepts.title: Apocalypse as Genre
concepts.summary: Apocalypse is a biblical genre of revelation, unveiling spiritual reality behind material events, not just the end of the world.

concepts.title: Reduction to Language
concepts.summary: Modern tendency to reduce all knowledge and experience to language, losing the fullness of noetic and ritual participation.

concepts.title: Cartesian Dualism
concepts.summary: The separation of material and spiritual realms, leading to a 'ghost in the machine' view of the soul and the natural/supernatural split.

concepts.title: Kantian and Hegelian Theology
concepts.summary: Kant's separation of noumenal and phenomenal realms, and Hegel's collapse of spirit into material, shaping conservative and liberal Western theology.

concepts.title: Liturgical Shaping
concepts.summary: The inflexible ritual of the liturgy shapes the nous, cleansing it to apprehend spiritual reality, unlike flexible worship that conforms to the individual.

concepts.title: Apocalypse of the Ordinary
concepts.summary: Every ordinary moment is an apocalyptic moment, revealing spiritual reality; the Christian life is holistic, with every action having spiritual significance.

claims.text: You are not your thoughts; the nous is a pre-reflective consciousness that can observe thoughts, enabling free will.
Descartes' 'I think therefore I am' is wrong because thinking is not what makes you you; the soul is not a ghost in the machine.
Modernity, through Cartesian dualism and Kantian/Hegelian philosophy, separated the material and spiritual realms, leading to secularism.
The whole Bible is apocalyptic, revealing spiritual reality behind material events, not just the book of Revelation.
God can work through worship outside the canonical Church, but we don't know how; we are accountable for what we receive.
Inflexible liturgy shapes the nous, cleansing it to see spiritual reality; flexible worship conforms to the individual and fails.
The only way to regain spiritual sight is through love of neighbor, not esoteric practices; love cleanses the nous.
